Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here's what he thinks of the iPhone 18 Pro variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Images, and more.

Stalman dives into the variable aperture camera of the iPhone 18 Pro

This year's iPhone 18 Pro brings a number of new features, including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, but the most exciting camera upgrade is without a doubt the variable aperture system.

Other updates include Cinematic mode, Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Images, and further refinements to professional controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shared his thoughts on all of the new hardware and software camera features of the iPhone 18 Pro. As the review embargo has lifted, reviews are pouring out from media outlets, including our own review over at 9to5Mac.

Stalman notes that while he really liked the Cosmic Orange color of last year's iPhone 17 Pro, it was prone to reflections when shooting through glass. Because of that, he recommends that professional photographers consider Deep Sea Blue or Black, as they are less likely to introduce unwanted color casts into photos and videos.

He also notes upfront that this review compares the camera of the iPhone 18 Pro against the iPhone 15 Pro, while the review video itself was shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

When it comes to the headlining upgrade for the main camera—the all-new variable aperture—Stalman says that the feature is a "huge leap forward in making the iPhone a real camera."

He also points out that the larger f/1.48 aperture allows more light to reach the sensor, which helps keep ISO lower in low-light situations and reduces how often Night mode kicks in.

This portion of the review shows off some great footage of the aperture blades opening and closing. Stalman mentions that one unique aspect of how Apple designed it is that the aperture blades sit in front of the main lens element, rather than being tucked deep within the optical stack as in traditional camera designs.

Stalman also notes that the 4x zoom on the iPhone 18 Pro (which was also a feature on last year's model) is a significant improvement over the 5x zoom on the iPhone 16 Pro, because the 5x focal length was sometimes a little too tight.

When it comes to features that may have "gone too far," he briefly mentions the new AI editing tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Re-Frame, noting that while they are technically impressive and quite convincing, they alter images so significantly that the final results lose the feel of the original.

When it comes to the iPhone 18 Pro's new texture options—Smooth Skin, Glow, and Film—Stalman demonstrates each option at different strengths from 0 to 100. His takeaway: Smooth Skin does a good job of subtly reducing skin texture without simply blurring skin tones; Glow produces a diffused, halated highlight effect similar to a professional Black Pro-Mist filter.

He was also impressed by the grain and halation of the Film mode, though he wishes Apple would give users more granular control over the intensity of the grain.

The review also covers Apple Reference Images, iPhone Cinematic mode (and why Stalman still recommends shooting with Apple Log for truly cinematic video), the new Apple Log 2, and intersperses photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.
